The 30-acre Brook Conservation Area, located on the Lynn River in the Southeast corner of Simcoe, provides opportunities for nature watching, fishing and hiking. At the entrance to the trail, one can see the remains of a shoddy mill that was once operated by the Brook family. The trail provides access to the Lynn River for fishing and links to the Lynn Valley Trail. Trails totalling 2.3 km go over a dam and through a forested area providing opportunities for walking/hiking, fishing and nature appreciation. The trail includes some hills and has a natural base with exposed tree roots.  A small picnic area with a few tables is available. The park is open sunrise to sunset and it should be noted that the entrance gate is locked each evening.

This gravel path connects two urban greenspaces and loops around natualized stormwater ponds.

This trail is located just east of the Whippoorwill Campground and takes you through an area of plantation and naturally forested areas that have had controlled fires (prescribed burns) to return the area to a natural oak and pine forest cover.

Begin at the north end of the Fin & Feather Campground and hike along the old hatchery pond to the Normandale Fish Hatchery, around to the north boundary of the park and then retrace the trail back into the park.

properties.DESCRIPTION: In Simcoe this trail meets up with the Norfolk Sunrise Trail, giving you the option of continuing on to Waterford, or heading towards Delhi. Starting at Silver Lake in Port Dover, you’ll pass sections of forest and grassland that will make you forget you’re in Southern Ontario. This trail is almost always covered by trees and shaded from the sun, with a few open areas near a grassland and a field. This trail passes over a number of rivers and creeks on beautiful old, well-maintained wooden foot bridges. In Simcoe, it meets up with the Norfolk Sunrise Trail at Victoria Street, just south of Clifton Park. This trail supports a variety of uses, including walking, running, biking, cross-country skiing, snowshoeing and is wheelchair accessible.

properties.DESCRIPTION: The Waterford Heritage Trail is a 19km old rail line trail that connects with the Brantford TH&B Rail Trail at Jenkins Road on the Norfolk and Brant County line. This section of the trail is part of the Trans Canada Trail and goes into Simcoe where it connects with the Norfolk Sunrise Trail. Gorgeous forests, fields, wetlands and grasslands line this rail trail, giving you a diverse landscape to view as you make your way into the town of Waterford. Here you’ll find the newly revamped Black Bridge; an old rail bridge that has been retrofitted specifically to connect the two ends of the Waterford Heritage trail. Black Bridge overlooks Waterford Ponds to the west, and to the east you can see the small downtown area looking picturesque with old buildings and trees. As you head out of Waterford toward Simcoe, you’ll pass through farmers’ fields and more forests before you connect with the Norfolk Sunrise Trail just outside of Simcoe. This trail supports a variety of activities including hiking, cycling, and cross-country skiing.

properties.DESCRIPTION: The Delhi Rail Trail is a 13.8km trail that takes you from the outskirts of Delhi into the heart of Simcoe, where it connects with the Norfolk Sunrise Trail, giving you the option to continue on to Port Dover or to Waterford. Passing through old fields, by farmhouses, and through forests, you’ll get a real sense of the landscape of the area. There are benches and bike stands at almost every trail access point to easily take breaks along the route. Before you get into Simcoe, you’ll pass by one of the area’s first solar farms, where solar panels stretch as far as the eye can see to the north.

A few connector trails provide relatively straight, easy access to neighbouring trails in the Turkey Point mountain bike trail system. Connections can be found between Dizzy Lizzy and Spinal Tap, between Wedomaker and Spinal Tap, and between Wedomaker and Humpback.

The Wilson Tract Trail in Norfolk County, Ontario, is part of the managed forest tracts in the Haldimand-Norfolk area. This trail offers a mix of doubletrack and singletrack paths, making it suitable for both hiking and mountain biking. The trail winds through beautiful Carolinian woods and can be linked with the Rowanwood Sanctuary for a longer hike. The area is known for its diverse bird and plant life, providing a serene environment for nature enthusiasts.

The Coppens Ferris Armstrong Tract Trail is part of the proposed Long Point Birding Trail in Norfolk County, Ontario. The are is wooded and offers a wonderful opportunity for hikers to enjoy birdwatching and observe various wildlife in their natural habitat. The area is known for its diverse ecosystems, making it a great spot for nature enthusiasts. The trail consists of a few out and back sections as well as loops from the north end.

properties.TRAIL_NAME: SWCR Nursery Tract Multi Use Trail
properties.TRAIL_USE: Hiking or Walking, Cycling, All-Terrain Vehicles (ATV), Off-Road Motorcycle
properties.DESCRIPTION: The Nursery Tract Multi-Use Trail at the St. Williams Conservation Reserve (SWCR) offers a versatile outdoor experience for various activities, including hiking, biking, horseback riding and ATV riding. The trail is designed to accommodate a range of activities, making it accessible for different types of users. The trail provides a well-maintained path through diverse natural habitats including forests, wetlands, and open fields, offering beautiful views and opportunities to observe local wildlife. The Nursery Tract Multi-Use Trail is part of the larger St. Williams Conservation Reserve, which is dedicated to restoring and enhancing native ecological communities.
properties.TRAIL_ASSOCIATION: St. Williams Conservation Reserve Community Council

properties.DESCRIPTION: This moderately difficult, singletrack trail traverses the valley running east-west while using the natural “spines” of the landscape. It is part of the greater Turkey Point Mountain Bike trail system offering a variety of trails for vaying skill levels.
This relatively straight, easy route provides access to the far side of the West Ridge sections of the Turkey Point mountain bike trail network.
This is an easy, out-and-back route, great for hiking, and it's unlikely you'll encounter many other people while exploring. Dogs are welcome.

This trail features a mix of gentle climbs and descents, making it suitable for riders of various skill levels. The trail includes several technical features such as jumps and rock gardens, and includes some great features including rock jumps and fast dips through the valley. Turkey Point offers over 85 kms of sandy and hardpacked cross country trails managed by the Turkey Point Mountain Bike Club (TPMBC) in association with several different landowners. This trail network is a hidden jewel and rideable most of the year.

This trail is part of the Walsingham Flats Conservation Area, which is known for its serene natural environment and diverse wildlife. The trail itself is an out-and-back route that is generally considered easy. It's a great spot for birding, cross-country skiing, and hiking. The area features a variety of trees, including American Sycamore and Black Walnut.

properties.TRAIL_USE: Hiking or Walking, Cycling, All-Terrain Vehicles (ATV), Off-Road Motorcycle
properties.DESCRIPTION: The Lions Trail is a scenic and accessible trail perfect for hiking and nature walks. This trail winds through a mix of forested areas and open spaces, offering a peaceful environment for visitors to enjoy. It's well-maintained and suitable for hikers of all skill levels, making it a great spot for a leisurely stroll or a more vigorous hike. The trail is known for its natural beauty and provides excellent opportunities for birdwatching and observing local wildlife.
properties.TRAIL_ASSOCIATION: Waterford Heritage Trails and Shadow Lake Park

properties.DESCRIPTION: This is an out and back trail that branch off the Mill Pond Trail to Backus Mill Road with a loop in the centre. These trails are located within the Backus Heritage Conservation Area.

This is a popular, moderately difficult, singletrack mountain bike trail. Turkey Point offers over 85 kms of sandy and hardpacked cross country trails managed by the Turkey Point Mountain Bike Club (TPMBC) in association with several different landowners. This trail network is a hidden jewel and rideable most of the year.

This is a popular, moderate difficulty, signle track mountain bike trail and enjoyable ride. Roughshod features a mix of natural terrain with roots and rocks, providing a fun and slightly technical experience for mountain bikers. The trail can be ridden in both directions and typically takes about 4 minutes to complete. It's a great choice for riders looking to improve their skills while enjoying the beautiful forested surroundings of Turkey Point. The trail is part of the Turkey Point Mountain Bike Trails network, which offers a variety of trails for different skill levels.

This is a challenging mountain biking trail known for its technical terrain. It is a singletrack trail thatcan be ridden in both directions, primarily used for mountain biking with a double black diamond difficulty rating. properties.TRAIL_USE: Hiking or Walking, Cross Country Skiing, Snowshoeing
properties.DESCRIPTION: Hike along a historic logging road to a spectacular view of High Falls; shared by both Ontario and Minnesota. Enjoy a view of Pigeon River’s steep walled gorge and visit the old chimney site. A plaque recognizing the Pigeon River as part of the Boundary Waters Voyageur Canadian Heritage River is located near the chimney site.  Across the river you will see the lookouts of Grand Portage State Park. High Falls is the highest waterfall in Minnesota (but not the highest in Ontario).

This trail takes hikers to a secluded sandy beach at Middlebrun Bay which is just 2.3km (4.6km round-trip) from the trailhead and is a great destination for those looking to soak up the sun, or even brave the frigid waters of Lake Superior. The trail continues to Finlay Bay where there is one designated backcountry campsite.
This trail provides access to the Sawyer Bay Trail from Marie Louise Lake Drive and includes a steep hill with partial views of Thunder Mountain.

The shortest trail in Sleeping Giant takes you over a bridge spanning Sibley Creek. Plantain Lane Nature Trail is wheelchair accessible and is conveniently located on Highway 587 near the Marie Louise Lake Campground.

The Tee Harbour Trail branches off the Kabeyun Trail and leads to a large outcrop jutting into Lake Superior. The total hike from the South Kabeyun Trailhead parking lot to the end of this trail and back is 12.4km. From the terminus of the trail, the boundless blue horizon of Lake Superior is only interrupted by a series of picturesque islands including Trowbridge Island, Silver Islet, and Isle Royal.

These well-maintained trails along the Eramosa River, providing scenic views and a tranquil environment within urban parks for walking and running. The trails are easy and accessible, with a mix of natural surfaces and paved paths. The total distance from the South Kabeyun Trailhead parking lot down Sawyer Bay Trail, across the Talus Lake Trail and back to the parking lot via the Kabeyun Trail is 18.6km. The Talus Lake Trail passes three secluded lakes, a sedge meadow, spectacular cliffs, talus slopes, and two cascading creeks. A portion of the trail travels over a boulder-field and another section crosses a beaver-dam. Proper trip planning and navigational skills are necessary to complete this challenging trail.

This short trail begins off Highway 587 and emerges at the Silver Islet Cemetery, one of two historical sites within Sleeping Giant Provincial Park. The nearby Silver Islet Mine operated from 1868 to 1884 and most of the graves found here date back to that period.
Wildlife Habitat Nature Trail consists of a series of three arcs that wind through dense brush and lead hikers to a seasonal pond.

This trail steadily ascends to a viewpoint that overlooks Grassy Lake, Lake Superior, and the Sibley Peninsula’s south-coast. The trail then travels down to the shore of Ravine Lake, returning through a shaded cedar grove.

A challenging mountain bike ride from Hwy 587 to the spectacular Thunder Bay Lookout. Many steep hills make it a treat to coast down on your return cycle. It is also part of Sleeping Giant's 50 km of groomed trails for cross-country skiers.

The steepest trail in the park climbs to the summit of the head of the Sleeping Giant. The lookout at the end of the trail is amongst the most astonishing viewpoints in the province. The total distance from the South Kabeyun Trailhead parking lot to the end of the Head Trail and back is 16.2km.

This challenging trail takes you to the top of the tallest cliffs in Ontario (greatest uninterrupted vertical drop) and provides access to some of the most breath-taking lookouts in central Canada. Spectacular views of both the east and west coast of the Sibley Peninsula are revealed to determined hikers who venture here. The total distance from the South Kabeyun Trailhead parking lot to the end of the Top of the Giant Trail and back is 21.8km and takes most hikers 6-10 hours to complete.

properties.TRAIL_NAME: Radial Line Trail: Smith Side Loop
properties.DESCRIPTION: The Radial Line Trail is one of three regional trails established and maintained by the Guelph Hiking Trail Club. This trail starts on the east side of the City of Guelph following an abandoned railway line to connect to the Bruce Trail near Limehouse. To learn more about this trail, including the history of the Guelph Radial Line Railway, pick up a copy of the Guelph Hiking Trail Club Handbook.  This map highlights one of the related side trails, named the Smith Side Trail. This loop trail is marked with blue blazes. The trail starts in Puslinch at Watson Road at an opening to the right of a large gate. Described in the Hiking Club handbook as a "very pleasant hike", in addition to following the abandoned railway bed, you will find a lookout over the Eramosa Valley, and the chance to hike through reforested areas and open meadows. The trails are primarily natural surface, providing a moderate difficulty level for hikers and nature enthusiasts through forests and natural areas in the Grand Rvier Conservation Area.

The Thunder Cape Trail branches off from the Kabeyun Trail at the feet of the Sleeping Giant and travels down a hill to the Thunder Cape Bird Observatory. This research station is outside of park boundaries and visitors to Thunder Cape Bird Observatory are reminded to be respectful of the ongoing research conducted there. The total distance from the South Kabeyun Trailhead parking lot to the Thunder Cape Bird Observatory and back is 23.2km. The Thunder Cape Trail itself is of moderate difficulty, however, there is a section on the approach-hike that involves difficult traversing of a talus slope below the knees of the Giant beyond Lehtinen’s Bay.

properties.TRAIL_USE: Hiking or Walking, Cross Country Skiing, Snowshoeing
properties.DESCRIPTION: The Bay’s End Lookout Trail (BELT) is part of the Trans-Canada Trail and connects Pass Lake to the Thunder Bay Lookout Road. The TCT in Ontario connects approximately 150 communities through a collection of linked multi use trails; giving preference to human-powered trail use. In Ontario many of the trails are greenway routes reserved for walking, hiking, running, and skiing; with cycling routes, paddling routes, and trail connections making up Ontario’s section of the coast to coast to coast trail network.

Located at km 37.6 - This demanding loop rewards the hiker with spectacular viewing along two high ridges.

This 10 kilometre leisurely trail runs along the abandoned rail bed of the historic Ottawa, Arnprior, and Parry Sound Railway built across the park in 1895. The trail has several interpretive panels along the route which explain Algonquin’s history.

Payne’s Pine Trail meanders through a section of the Little Bonnechere where the nature of the north meets the nature of the south. As you head out, note the jack pine and red pine which have been planted on this abandoned homestead. Jack pine, among the most common trees of the northern boreal forest, quickly establishes itself following fires, insect outbreaks and – with some help – logging activities. The trail skirts a spruce bog environment. Black spruce, sphagnum moss, pitcher plants, sundew and cottongrass are typical inhabitants of vast bogs such as this that cloak much of northern Ontario. Watch for moose, spruce grouse, gray jays and black-backed woodpeckers, which are also northern species. At this spot you may be lucky enough to encounter white-tailed deer which, in contrast, are more common to the south. Payne’s Pine Trail eventually leads to a bayou-like silver maple swamp on the banks of the Little Bonnechere River. This lush green habitat is very reminiscent of flooded swamps of Rondeau Provincial Park, in Ontario’s Carolinian Zone on the north shore of Lake Erie, and points further south.

The Minnesing Mountain Bike Trail is located 23 km from the West Gate and 33 km from the East Gate, just off of Hwy 60.  The trail is hilly and unsuitable for small children and unfit adults. It is rated at a moderate level of technical difficulty. The western or return side follows the old Minnesing Road where the trail is smoother and the grades are less steep. Expect extensive muddy sections until the drier weather of August and September. Cabins are located at the start of the trail and on the return run of the second loop. The trail passes through hardwood forest with views of three lakes along the way. During the winter months this trail is used for backcountry wilderness skiing and is not groomed. Wide touring skis and large basket poles are essential for soft snow conditions. This trail network is very challenging and is only recommended for experienced skiers who are well prepared for the conditions.To minimize damage to trails, dogs, walking, snowshoeing, toboggans and sleighs are not permitted on ski trails.

Following the close of the American Revolution in the late 1700's, Upper Canada became a haven for United Empire Loyalists escaping the United States, many of whom made their way from Niagara to the western end of Lake Ontario where they had been granted land by King George III of England. Attracted by the potential water power offered by the Spencer Creek, many early settlers came to this area of Flamborough West. It was to this particular area that two early families came, the Mordens and the Crooks. The HCA owns and manages several properties in the Crooks' Hollow area. A 1.5-kilometre self-guiding trail past early homes, and the ruins of barns, sawmills and water-control devices can be found at Crooks' Hollow Conservation Area parking lot, just off Crooks' Hollow Road.

properties.DESCRIPTION: Accessed through North Lumby Campground, or through the Arrowhead Lake Trail. Completing both Arrowhead Lake and the Beaver Meadow loop will be 9 km. This trail passes Porcupine Bluffs, the remnant shoreline of a huge ancient lake. The bluffs are easily visible in the spring and fall but are hidden during the leafy summer months. The trail circles a large beaver pond with large rafts of cattails where you might see otter, moose, Great Blue Heron, Tree Swallows and, of course, beavers. Near the end, the trail crosses a field, and you can see evidence of the once successful Oke homestead—old fence lines, building foundations and domestic plants such as rhubarb and apple trees. This trail is a part of the ski trail system in the winter.

Ten thousand years ago, Mayflower Lake was a small bay in a large glacial lake. Today it is a small, deep, spring-fed lake. Its cold, clear waters provide ideal habitat for cold water fish such as Rainbow Trout. This trail has several lengthy climbs and descents over the hills surrounding Mayflower Lake and can be muddy, so wear your hiking boots. This trail turns into a snowshoeing trail in the winter.

Take an easy stroll along the meandering Bonnechere River and learn about its rich natural and cultural history by exploring our Foot Prints in Time (FIT). FIT is based on the traditional local First Nations way of teaching and explaining our history. The trail takes you in stride with 13 giant foot prints, marked by posts with interpretive and educational text designed to be informative and engage you and your family along the hike. You will truly enjoy this adventure.

The Arrowhead Lake Trail winds around the perimeter of Arrowhead’s major lake! The trail can be used for hiking and biking and turns into one of our most popular cross country ski trails in the winter. At 5.1 km in length, the trail takes approximately 1.5-2 hours to walk and 30-45 minutes to bike. The Arrowhead Plant, the park’s namesake, is visible along the shorelines. The trail provides some great vistas overlooking the lake and a wetland where Great Blue Herons are often seen.

From the accessible parking area near the Admin Building at the entrance to Bonnechere Provincial Park, pick up the trailhead. The Nòpiming FIT Trail provides accessible hiking opportunities in a quiet woodland environment. This barrier free trail features a medicine wheel, benches, guide ropes, and a limestone screenings surface. Bikes are not permitted on the trail. Inquire about renting an all terrain wheelchair for trail use at the park store.
